procedural_history.originating_court: P.S. Motiganj, District Gonda (implied, as the case originated from a police station)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 22.07.2015 of the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench, Lucknow in Cr!. Misc. Petition No. 1392 of 2008.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a Writ Petition No. 2330 (M/B) of 2007 before the High Court, which stayed their arrest on 13.04.2007. Subsequently, they filed a petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. (Cr!. Misc. Petition No. 1392 of 2008) to quash the proceedings of Criminal Case No. 531 of 2007. The High Court dismissed this petition, finding no illegality in the charge sheet and stating that charges cannot be quashed piecemeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants, aggrieved by the High Court's order dated 22.07.2015 in Cr!. Misc. Petition No. 1392 of 2008, appealed to the Supreme Court. This is evidenced by the case being a Criminal Appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 2039 of 2017) before the Supreme Court.

directions: The Supplementary Report filed by the Police, at the direction of the Commission, is quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court can exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash a chargesheet in part.

facts: The appellants challenged a supplementary chargesheet by filing a petition under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC) in the High Court.
The High Court dismissed the petition, stating that a chargesheet cannot be quashed in a "piecemeal manner."
The appellants appealed this decision to the Supreme Court.
law: Under Section 482 of the CrPC, the High Court has inherent power to intervene to secure the ends of justice, prevent abuse of the process of law, or implement orders under the CrPC.
The Supreme Court explicitly stated that there is "no prohibition under law for quashing a chargesheet in part."
A person may be accused of several offenses but can be aggrieved by only a particular charge or set of charges, and they are entitled to challenge just those specific charges.
A chargesheet filed at the dictate of an external body, rather than as a result of the police's own investigation, constitutes an abuse of the process of law.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the High Court's role under Section 482 is to determine if its intervention is necessary to prevent an abuse of process or secure justice.
It found that if a specific part of a chargesheet results from an abuse of process, the High Court has the power and a duty to quash that part, without having to quash the entire document.
In this specific case, the supplementary report was filed at the direction of the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, which the Court deemed an abuse of process.
Therefore, the High Court should have exercised its jurisdiction to quash the abusive part of the chargesheet (the supplementary report).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was incorrect in its view. It held that there is no legal bar to quashing a chargesheet in part and that the High Court ought to have exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 CrPC to quash the supplementary report, as it was an abuse of the legal process.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court can exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code to quash a chargesheet in part.
appellant_arguments: The appellants argued that the High Court should have exercised its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the CrPC to quash the supplementary chargesheet.
They contended that the High Court's view that charges cannot be quashed in a piecemeal manner was incorrect.
Specifically, they argued that no case was made out under Section 3(1)(x) of the SC/ST Act, which was added via the supplementary chargesheet.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's argument, in line with the High Court's judgment, was that the chargesheet cannot be quashed in a piecemeal manner.

cases.case_name: R. Sarala v. T. S. Velu & Ors.
cases.principle: The High Court has jurisdiction under s.482 to quash a chargesheet in part to secure the ends of justice, as there is no prohibition in law against it. Additionally, no external agency can dictate the course of a criminal investigation, which is within the exclusive jurisdiction of the police.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: No external agency can dictate the course of investigation in a criminal case, as it falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the police.
obiter: The order passed by this Court shall not stand in the way of the police and for that matter the Court, taking any steps in due exercise of their powers under the provisions of the CrPC, if so warranted, at any stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: There is no legal prohibition against quashing a chargesheet in part. A person may be accused of several distinct offenses but only be aggrieved by the prosecution of a particular charge or charges. In such cases, the High Court ought to exercise its jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code to examine if its intervention is necessary to secure the ends of justice, and it can quash specific charges without dismissing the entire chargesheet.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the High Court is required to examine whether its intervention is required for implementing orders under the CrPC, for prevention of abuse of process, or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
policy_considerations: The power under Section 482 CrPC should be exercised to secure the ends of justice, which includes allowing an accused person to challenge only a particular charge or charges on any ground available to them in law, rather than forcing them to face prosecution for baseless charges simply because other charges in the same chargesheet may be valid.
The intervention of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC is necessary for the prevention of abuse of process.
